column4: Table 1 of H-37232-3: tensile modulus by ASTM D 882, machine direction 490 kg/mm^2 and transverse direction 510 kg/mm^2 (4805.2585 and 5001.3915 MPa with 1 kgf = 9.80665 N); density 1.390 g/cm^3 by ASTM D 1505; page 2: Poisson's ratio is typically 0.38 before yield
column5: Typical performance data, which the bulletin says are not intended to be used as design data. Table 1 states no test temperature; the rows are admitted for 20 to 23 C (ASTM D 882's standard laboratory atmosphere is 23 C), where Matsuzawa's resonance moduli, which fall by about 4 percent from 15 to 30 C (his Fig. 5), bound the unknown test temperature's effect to about 1 percent. Drum heads are 7.5 to 10 mil (0.19 to 0.25 mm) films, thicker than this gauge, and the modulus is carried to them without thickness data. isotropic head: E = mean(MD, TD); MD/TD = 4805.2585 / 5001.3915 MPa (+/- 2.0 %), the isotropic young_modulus being the pack author's reduction (500 kg/mm^2 = 4903.325 MPa), not a datasheet value; the spread is the size of the error an isotropic head makes; the film's 4 percent in-plane anisotropy is not represented by it. This is a quasi-static tensile modulus: Matsuzawa 1959 found the Young's modulus of Mylar film independent of frequency within measurement error from about 100 to 4000 Hz at every temperature from 15 to 90 C, the basis for using it in vibration; no frequency axis is claimed. The pack makes NO loss claim: no frequency-dependent loss of biaxially oriented PET film in the audio band was found in a citable source
